newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: EnerTel says has head start in Dutch phones market.
newsitem.headline: EnerTel says has head start in Dutch phones market.

text.p: EnerTel, a group of utilities and cable tv companies which has applied for a new Dutch fixed telecoms licence, said on Monday its existing infrastructure could give it a strong advantage while the government comes to a decision.
The Netherlands has received applications from three groups, including EnerTel, for a possible two fixed telephony licences allowing competition with current monopolist Dutch PTT.
"We have more infrastructure than anyone else, more than (competitor) Telfort," EnerTel NV Managing Director Ad Ketelaars said in an interview.

Last week British Telecommunications Plc and Dutch state owned rail company Nederlandse Spoorwegen named their new Dutch telecoms venture Telfort and said they planned a one billion guilder ($588.4 million) investment over the next four or five years.
The third competitor for a high profile role in the Dutch telecoms market is Global One, a joint venture of Sprint Corp, France Telecom and Deutsche Telekom.
A decision on the licences is expected by the year-end.
"We have 5,000 kilometres of optical fibre whereas Telfort has 1,000. On top of that we have 70 percent of the Dutch cable TV households -- that's 3.7 million," said Ketelaars.

"There are two licences to be given and there are three applicants. We think we will get the licence. One of the comparisons between the applicants as to whether you get the licence or not is the extent to which you're using existing infrastructure in Holland," said Ketelaars.

EnerTel has a solid backbone in the Randstad conurbation which groups the main Dutch cities including Amsterdam, The Hague, Rotterdam and Utrecht. Added to this are regional loops built up to carry the cable and utilities firms' own telecoms.

And the company's cable TV links to the bulk of Dutch consumers gives it big possibilities in building up the local loop, although Ketelaars said EnerTel would take a step by step approach in rolling out to the consumer market.
The EnerTel group is also looking for a one billion guilder investment over the coming years, but that could rise to between two and four billion over 10 years as expansion develops.
Ketelaars, who is targeting 15 percent of the market by the year 2005, is convinced the Dutch market can support three major telecoms operators.

"There is a place for three operators...but it's the most logical expectation that KPN (Dutch PTT) will be the biggest carrier," he said, pointing out that BT still had the bulk of the British market 12 years after privatisation.
"PTT Telecom is a competitor you shouldn't underestimate, so you cannot make plans that go through the roof, you have to go step by step," Ketelaars said.
EnerTel was looking for a different place in the market to Telfort which he said would be looking to promote BT's Concert portfolio of services aimed at big multinational companies.
"We are offering more national products to somewhat smaller customers not targeted by BT," he said.

"The EnerTel mission is to sell to the top corporate customers in Holland a broad portfolio of services. To be an interconnect "carrier's carrier" for all regional carriers whether they are part of us or part of others," he said.
The regional carriers sell towards small and medium sized businesses and to consumers and EnerTel facilitates this by providing a common technology and marketing approach.
Further ahead EnerTel plans to offer consumers links through upgraded cable TV lines, two different types of wireless telephony and an "easy access" system using capacity on Dutch PTT's circuits.
But Ketelaars sounded a note of caution about full blooded expansion into the local loop. "You can imagine that that isn't a decision you take overnight," he said.

New developments and products in telephony -- including broad band internet and video related developments -- would keep the market growing, providing pickings for new telecoms players although prices would continue to fall over the years.

"The market will grow because the applications will grow. Prices will go down but because of the increase in applications there will be growth," said Ketelaars. -- Amsterdam Newsroom +31 20 504 5000 ($ = 1.699 Dutch Guilders)
